title: Brushing & Flossing
meta_title: Brushing & Flossing That Actually Works | West Alexandria Dental Care
meta_description: Home care advice from West Alexandria Dental Care: technique, electric vs manual, floss and its alternatives, timing around acids, and how to clean crowns.
h1: Brushing and flossing that actually works
intro: Most people brush twice a day and still get cavities and bleeding gums. The problem is rarely effort. It is technique, timing and the places that get missed. Here is what we tell patients in the chair, written down.

items.title: Soft brush, light grip
items.body: Hold it like a pen, not a fist. Hard brushes and hard scrubbing wear away gum and enamel at the neck of the tooth, which is where most sensitivity starts. If your bristles splay within a month, you are pressing too hard.

items.title: Angle at the gum line
items.body: Tilt the bristles about forty-five degrees toward the gum so they slip just under the edge. That is where plaque collects and where gum disease begins. Small circles or short back-and-forth strokes, a few teeth at a time.

items.title: Every surface, in order
items.body: Outside, inside and chewing surfaces, upper and lower. Most people miss the inside of the lower front teeth and the back of the last molars. Working in the same order every time stops that.

items.title: Two minutes, by the clock
items.body: Most people guess at forty-five seconds. Use a timer or an electric brush with one built in.

items.title: Spit, do not rinse
items.body: Rinsing with water washes the fluoride away. Spit out the excess and leave the film.

sections.heading: Electric or manual?
rows: Does the motion; you guide it slowly along the gum line
Many have a sensor that warns you
Most adults, anyone with dexterity limits, teenagers who rush
People with good technique who prefer it

sections.heading: Cleaning between the teeth
sections.intro: A brush cleans three of the five surfaces of a tooth. The two that touch neighbors need something else, once a day.

items.title: Floss
items.body: Wrap it around each tooth in a C shape and slide it gently below the gum line on both sides of the gap. Snapping it straight down and up does little.

items.title: Interdental brushes
items.body: Tiny bristle brushes in several sizes. Better than floss for larger gaps, around bridges, braces and implants, and easier for many people to use well.

items.title: Water flossers
items.body: A good option for people who will not floss, for braces, and around implants and bridges. Aim at the gum line, not straight at the gum.

items.title: Floss picks
items.body: Convenient and better than nothing. The angle makes it harder to curve around the tooth, so use them carefully.

sections.heading: Timing and diet
items: Wait about thirty minutes after acidic food or drink before brushing. Enamel is softened by acid and brushing it then wears it away.
Sip water, not sparkling water, juice or sports drinks, through the day. Frequency of acid matters more than amount.
Brush last thing at night and do not eat afterward. Saliva drops during sleep and the teeth have no defense.
Sugar-free gum after meals stimulates saliva and helps neutralize acid.
Clean your tongue with the brush or a scraper. It holds most of the bacteria behind bad breath.

items.title: Crowns and bridges
items.body: The edge where crown meets tooth is where decay starts. Brush it deliberately and thread floss under a bridge with a floss threader or use an interdental brush.

items.title: Implants
items.body: Implants do not decay but the gum around them can get infected. Floss or interdental brushes daily and keep up maintenance visits.

items.title: Aligners
items.body: Brush and floss after every meal before the trays go back in, and clean the trays with a soft brush and cool water, never hot.

items.title: Dentures
items.body: Out at night, brushed with a denture brush and soaked. Brush the gums, tongue and palate with a soft brush too.

items.title: Children
items.body: A parent brushes or checks until about age seven or eight. A rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste under three, a pea from three to six.

items.title: Sensitive teeth
items.body: A desensitizing toothpaste used consistently for several weeks, a soft brush and light pressure. Scrubbing sensitive roots makes them worse.

sections.heading: Bleeding when you floss?
sections.body: Bleeding is a sign of inflamed gums, not a reason to stop. Keep flossing gently every day and it usually settles within two weeks. If it does not, or if gums bleed when you brush, that is worth an appointment.

faqs.a: No. It does not replace brushing or cleaning between the teeth. A fluoride rinse used at a separate time can help people at higher cavity risk. Alcohol-based rinses dry the mouth and are best avoided if dry mouth is already a problem.

faqs.q: Should I brush before or after breakfast?
faqs.a: Either, as long as you wait thirty minutes after anything acidic like juice or coffee before brushing. Many people find brushing before breakfast simpler.

faqs.q: How often should I replace my toothbrush?
faqs.a: Every three months, or sooner if the bristles splay. A worn brush cleans poorly, and splayed bristles usually mean too much pressure.

faqs.q: Is charcoal or whitening toothpaste a good idea?
faqs.a: Charcoal pastes are abrasive and can wear enamel without whitening it. Whitening pastes remove surface stain only. For real whitening, see our teeth whitening page. For daily use, an ordinary fluoride paste is the right choice.
